newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Hopes for Zaire truce fade, refugees roam bush.
newsitem.headline: Hopes for Zaire truce fade, refugees roam bush.

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila dimmed hopes for a ceasefire in Zaire's civil war by rejecting South African and U.S. pressure for a deal.

In his clearest public statement about secret talks in Cape Town last week, he said he refused to sign an agreement to end the four-month-old conflict in which his declared goal is to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Kabila told a news conference in the eastern town of Goma that his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo was making steady progress on the battlefield, capturing the strategic town of Lubutu.
He appealed to the United Nations to help some 170,000 refugees who fled the nearby camp of Tingi Tingi but insisted there could be no truce without direct negotiations with Mobutu.
"The alliance waits for an invitation saying that Mobutu has written to the organisers (of talks) to say that he personally will negotiate. Only then will we negotiate," Kabila said.
South African President Nelson Mandela met Kabila and an aide to Mobutu last week in an attempt to broker peace.
Mobutu, now in France ailing with prostate cancer, has decided to delay his return home for a few days to pursue his search for a solution to the crisis, an aide said.
His government has consistently ruled out talks with Kabila, whom it terms a puppet in the hands of Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi, seen by Zaire as the real aggressors.
Kabila said his forces overran the makeshift Tingi Tingi refugee camp on Saturday, dislodging Rwandan and Burundian refugees who had fled fighting further east.

The Tingi Tingi refugees are said to include members of the Interahamwe militia and former Rwandan government army held responsible for the 1994 Rwanda genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Aid workers said the refugees were apparently now trying to reach Kisangani or nearby Ubundu.

"They are heading in two different groups, one towards the town of Ubundu and the other towards Kisangani. From the air it apeared that there were no more refugees left at Tingi Tingi," an aid worker said.

The relief workers in Kinshasa were quoting colleagues flew over the Tingi Tingi area when they were evacuated by plane from the town of Bunia. They said the plane was shot at with automatic weapons over the camp.
U.N. relief agencies who withdrew from their headquarters in Kisangani on Saturday defended their decision, denounced by Zaire as creating panic in the region.
They said in a statment that their pullout was based on assessments of "operational difficulties...coupled with a severe deterioration in local security conditions."
The statement cited frequent seizures of humanitarian transport by local military authorities and harassment of aid workers by European mercenaries backing the Zaire army.
Kabila suggested that aid agencies would be able to fly into Tingi Tingi immediately to encourage refugees to return.

"Many hundreds of refugees are coming and our men have been ordered not to harm them...The United Nations is invited to go to Tingi Tingi to help the refugees to return home and help repatriate them," he said.
Doctors have said up to 40 refugees a day are dying of hunger or disease.
Kabila's forces control most of eastern Zaire after launching a war in October to oust Mobutu, in power since 1965.
Lubutu, 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Kisangani, is the last town on the road from Bukavu, the first major town to fall to the rebels in the war.
